title: Big Tech’s War on Human Achievement
author: Gregory Conti
content:
![Big Tech’s War on Human
Achievement](https://storage.ghost.io/c/65/af/65afbdb5-30bf-4286-acc4-9535069adb42/content/images/2026/07/Screenshot-2026-07-26-at-10.08.59
---PM.png)

Just a couple weeks ago, Secretary of State Marco Rubio made conservatives
cheer when he delivered a sharp rebuke to communism not only for the
atrocities committed in its name, but for the picture of human life underlying
it:

> One of the criticisms you sometimes hear of communism, for example, is that
> it sounds good in theory, but it never works in practice. That's actually
> not true. Communism does not sound good in theory. The world it envisions
> for all of us is small, flat, grey, leveled of all exception, drained of all
> that is good and noble in the human soul. The world it envisions is a world
> without courage, a world without creativity or ambition, a world without
> heroes or glory or great causes to strive towards, without--a world without
> miracles, without myths, without men who rise above the rest to do
> incredible and extraordinary things.

Communism, according to Rubio, would not be laudable if only we could make it
work, because making it work would mean an end of great individual
accomplishment and of the striving that brings romance and meaning to our
lives.

The trouble is, as I was reading this, it _did_ sound like a depiction of a
very live ideology that is one of the most powerful forces in the United
States today. I refer not to communism, but to the ideology of technological
succession, or transhumanism, that is guiding our AI entrepreneurs. Every word
of Rubio's castigation of communism could apply even more fully to the views
of an industry to which his administration is extremely close.

Communism is not going to overrun America, the recent electoral surge of the
DSA notwithstanding. But the grand ambitions of our Silicon Valley tycoons
very well may do so. For despite a recent attempt to turn the messaging more
upbeat as AI takes a pummeling in public opinion, the fact is that the
architects of artificial intelligence explicitly envision a world from which
distinctions based on effort and ability are absent. Their stated mission is
to create artificial general intelligence: an AI system that is more capable
than human beings along most or all cognitive dimensions and that is able to
perform the vast bulk of economically useful work. In other words, a world in
which there is no opportunity for individuals to distinguish themselves via
skill and effort, because these things will have been rendered irrelevant.

> "These things will have been rendered irrelevant."

This is the vision articulated in Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei's essay [_"
Machines of Loving Grace_](https://darioamodei.com/essay/machines-of-loving-
grace?ref=compactmag.com)," among many other works from this milieu--a vision
that his colleague [_Jack
Clark_](https://x.com/jackclarkSF/status/1962271034998194350?ref=compactmag.com)
assures us is realizable by the end of this year. Elon Musk is slightly more
modest (rare to say of him), for [_he
claims_](https://www.youtube.com/watch?app=desktop&v=adgbH9FixW0&ref=compactmag.com)
that we're a still few years away from AI that will be "unequivocally smarter
than humans in every way," meaning that "digital intelligence will exceed the
sum of all human intelligence." Going beyond the worst that anyone could
allege of communism, our AI leadership envisions a world in which humanity no
longer occupies the driver's seat of history. A world of boredom, idleness,
and mere consumption awaits us, for it is the machines that will henceforth
solve all the problems we face.

The idea that human beings may soon be surpassed along every cognitive
dimension seems too far-fetched to be true. But sadly, it is a very real
possibility--as those who follow the astonishing progress that generative and
agentic AI have made in the past few years are aware. For any skeptics, I
recommend the journalist Garrison Lovely's exhaustively researched
[_forthcoming
book_](https://orbooks.com/catalog/obsolete/?ref=compactmag.com), which
documents what he aptly dubs the "obsoleting project" that animates our AI
companies: the goal of discarding human labor of all kinds by producing more
efficient AI systems. As Lovely shows, every AI leader has publicly spoken of
the future they are bringing about as one in which there will be no place for
human excellence, or even real human action. Amodei has [_been
frank_](https://darioamodei.com/essay/the-adolescence-of-
technology?ref=compactmag.com) that what he is creating is "a general labor
substitute for humans," his own role as a tech CEO not excepted from this
process of becoming an anachronism. As one __[_OpenAI
employee_](https://x.com/zetalyrae/status/2080056964126822536?ref=compactmag.com)
admitted last week: he "would prefer a world of rapid RSI [recursive self-
improvement, where AI models train their own successors without any human
involvement] and human disempowerment." Next to the money and power and
effectiveness of this project of technological replacement, communism in
America barely registers.

Moreover, this vision of dispensing with human effort and activity is not just
an ideology, but increasingly our reality. In my world of academia, we are
witnessing with astonishing speed a world in which AI proliferates _findings_
but discards the _finders_. In mathematics, [_the
pace_](https://github.com/teorth/erdosproblems/wiki/AI-contributions-to-
Erd%C5%91s-problems?ref=compactmag.com) at which the latest AI models [_have
improved_](https://x.com/aibattle_/status/2080713358366445687?s=46&ref=compactmag.com)
has become almost a source of comedy on twitter, and has led [_a recent
winner_](https://www.ams.org/journals/notices/202607/noti3372/noti3372.html?ref=compactmag.com)
of the subject's highest honor, the Fields medal, to declare that soon math as
a field of human endeavor will be gone. (He has since decided to leave
mathematics behind to work on [_AI
safety_](https://www.binance.com/en/square/post/07-24-2026-fields-medalist-
jacob-tsimerman-joins-openai-for-ai-safety-
research-348186081210994?ref=compactmag.com).) Likewise, [_another leading
light_](https://www.reddit.com/r/accelerate/comments/1v0vb2t/fields_medalist_timothy_gowers_expects_the_2030/?ref=compactmag.com)
of mathematics suggests that the next time the quadrennial Fields is given, it
will be the last, for by the early 2030s humans will simply be outcompeted
across the board in mathematics. The pace of AI discoveries in the field was
emblematized by the
[_announcement_](https://x.com/Joshuwa/status/2080472449682944209?ref=compactmag.com)
that a two-decades-old problem was solved by ChatGPT while its user "took a
nap." This looks like a metaphor of intellectual life writ large going
forward: miraculous results while humanity slumbers.

It is not just in pure math that AI is making significant inroads. Arguably
[_the most important open
problem_](https://x.com/wfithian/status/2077218361398964684?ref=compactmag.com)
in statistics was solved by GPT 5.6. Some academics
[_believe_](https://www.popularbydesign.org/p/academics-need-to-wake-up-on-
ai?utm_campaign=posts-open-in-app&triedRedirect=true&ref=compactmag.com) that
AI "can already do social science research better than most professors."
Likewise, leading commentators think [_the
humanities_](https://www.persuasion.community/p/the-humanities-are-about-to-
be-automated?ref=compactmag.com) are not far behind. One particular
[_intellectual
entrepreneur_](https://x.com/jmrphy/status/2079686184242999591?ref=compactmag.com)
is certain that automation will imminently suffuse the process of composition
for even the most accomplished writers--and happily, due to technological
advances, this substitution of AI for human authorship will be completely
undetectable. By some metrics AI is already outperforming
[_doctors_](https://www.science.org/content/article/ai-starting-beat-doctors-
making-correct-diagnoses?ref=compactmag.com) and
[_lawyers_](https://law.stanford.edu/press/ai-outperforms-law-professors-in-
stanford-law-study/?ref=compactmag.com). We may well be, many serious people
think, in the twilight years of intellectual endeavor by "meatsuits" at all.

From my own experience, I have been astonished at the capacity of the latest
models. While Claude can't write papers that are at the top level yet, it can
do frankly amazing things. I recently uploaded some relevant primary sources
and prodded Claude a bit in the direction of an article I was intending to
write, and I was amazed at how close its conclusions got, in a matter of
minutes, to what I was intending to argue. It was phenomenally deflating.
_What was now the point of all the exertions for knowledge and know-how that
had taken up countless years of my life? What do I still have to offer?_
--these were among the questions that occurred to me on this and other recent
instances. In these feelings I am [_hardly
alone_](https://kirwinhampshire.substack.com/p/the-dark-night-of-
mathematics?ref=compactmag.com), and when one allows that the tech, if allowed
to proceed, is only going to improve, it is only a matter of time until
everyone is asking themselves something similar in their own domains.

* * *

On our current trajectory, humanity's intellectual horizon is set to shrink
dramatically. What has begun in mathematics and academic work will not stay
there--unless we move to pause frontier development imminently. For every
problem solved by AI, that is one fewer arena in which a person, through their
diligence and hard work and intellect, can shine. The idea that humans are
great rational and cognitive beings, that we are not just a bundle of emotions
and feelings, will itself fade into obscurity. The channels for the human mind
to swim in will dry up, one-by-one--and perhaps much more quickly than we are
prepared for. The opportunities for a man to feel the satisfaction of a "job
well done" will disappear. As AI continues its stunning progress, the night
comes when no man can work.

AI means the death of authorship--and of the inspiration that work which you
know reflects human achievement, and human competence, provides to all who
read it. We will increasingly become mere "prompters," at best "collaborators"
with the machine. As sci-fi as it sounds, we are already well on our way to
becoming mere interchangeable vessels for ChatGPT's accomplishments and
insights. The awe that we feel in reflecting on an Einstein or a Dostoevsky,
we will feel toward no one again; Claude cannot be someone's hero. The whole
concept of a "life's work" that belongs to a great progenitor of ideas is
under threat; soon we may have less reason to care who "wrote" a paper with an
AI's help or who inaugurated a theory by prompting Claude than we do about who
was riding Secretariat when he won his triple crown.

So far, the progress of science, the accomplishments of literature, have gone
hand-in-hand with the _formation_ of scientists and writers. But that
consonance between human type and achieving a result has now been broken. The
future we are looking at is one of more science but fewer, or no, scientists.
[_Astrophysics without
astrophysicists_](https://www.science.org/content/article/amid-flood-ai-
advances-astrophysicists-are-questioning-soul-their-field?ref=compactmag.com),
history without historians--this is the future. But this is a deeply sad
future, for what we have wanted from these fields--and many more, including
law and medicine and government--is not just a set of outcomes, but the
production of a kind of person who we think is valuable, and therefore the
realization of a form of flourishing. We have always wanted to produce not
just poetry, but poets; not just education, but teachers; not just policy, but
statesmen; not just films, but actors; not just music, but musicians. A
chatbot cannot love knowledge or feel the weight of responsibility for a
domain or discipline; it is not one of us whom we can admire and emulate. Who
cares if AI delivers discoveries that surpass our understanding, or generates
reams of new historical writing but in so doing saps our ability to cherish
and devote ourselves to history? Such a stance of devotion is itself only
possible through the long grappling and struggle that AI will extinguish.

This dawn of the AI age has made it painfully clear to me that what moves me
is not raw output but the human effort to find new truths, follow through in
difficult undertakings, master a craft. If one looks at biopics of
politicians, artists, inventors, it is evident that this human-all-too-human-
drama is what most of us care about most deeply. As we produce various results
and effects in the world, we are also shaping ourselves, carrying out a
valuable life's work. But all this will be gone if AI keeps marching forward.
For every time a prompt is given to AI that results in a problem being solved,
humanity (including the prompter) has been robbed of the chance to solve it on
its own, and to display virtues and excellences along the way.

Consider what becomes of philosophy under the reign of AI. For philosophy is
not just a set of conclusions, but a way of life. Etymologically, philosophy
refers to the love of wisdom. In this sense no matter how elegant and cogent
its interventions, Grok can never be a philosopher, for it cannot have that
disposition of love, it cannot have a will to live according to the truth. So
as AI advances we won't have philosophy without philosophers; philosophy will
simply die, whatever tonnage of words on the subject the machines keep
churning out.

A final way to think about the tragedy of AI advancing beyond us is that it
spells the end of the possibility of having a vocation. That we are elevated
above mere animalistic consumption by consistent work in a calling is one of
the deepest features of civilized life; far from belonging only to geniuses,
many who toil in complete anonymity get much of their satisfaction and sense
of self from feeling that they are making a contribution through their work.
As soon as AI gets the better of us, though, that feeling will be an
unsustainable illusion; if one can press the enter key and get the same or
better outcomes, then no one will be able to sustain the conception that their
work _matters_. For it is the characteristic of a vocation that the moral
goods it brings are what [_the philosopher Jon
Elster_](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs/sour-grapes/states-that-are-
essentially-byproducts/9CE2D6D6B587B7FFE245F2E15F67654D?ref=compactmag.com)
calls "states that are essentially byproducts." A surgeon gets a great sense
of purpose from his work because he believes he is actually healing the sick.
If he practiced surgery, however, directly to gain a sense of purpose and
without any concern about his own efficacy in making us healthy, he would fail
to gain such contentment. To engage in something without thinking the outcome
makes a difference is to enter the realm of play, of hobbies and games--which
is what a number of commentators think is all that will be left to human
beings in the AI age. As the journalist [_Jasmine
Sun_](https://www.dialectic.fm/jasmine-sun?ref=compactmag.com) puts it, due to
the progress of AI "everything is going to become a little bit more like
playing board games soon." The work ethic, the conviction that through your
labor you are making a mark on the world, are _contributing_ to creating some
important results--this will be the first casualty of an age in which AI
exceeds human capabilities.

> "Human beings weren't made to have only hobbies."

Human beings weren't made to have only hobbies. We need, even more, to have
vocations. The nature of the latter is that the pleasure comes not merely from
the doing itself but from the idea that one is making a real contribution--in
theological language, that God called you to it because your work there was
necessary. But as soon as the machines can do what we do better than we
ourselves can, the conditions for our having a vocation cease to exist.
Instead, we will have only play, mere amusements--we will be like pets, as the
economist [_Noah Smith_](https://www.thefp.com/p/you-are-no-longer-the-
smartest-type?ref=compactmag.com) says. This would be the biggest change in
the history of the species, and would mark a demoralization far greater than
anything that communism caused. It would truly be a world that is "small,
flat, grey, leveled of all exception, drained of all that is good and noble."
And it very well may come, and come soon, unless we consciously stop it.
